items.stem: A student claims: "P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) always." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.

items.stem: A game at a festival in Geneva costs CHF 1. You win CHF 2 with probability 0.04 and CHF 50 with probability 0.04; otherwise nothing. Find the expected winnings and the expected gain per game. Is the game fair?

items.stem: A survey of 28 tourists in Singapore found that 12 visited the museum, 16 visited the zoo and 2 visited neither. Let A = "visited the museum" and B = "visited the zoo". (a) Draw a Venn diagram and find every region. (b) Find the probability that one of the tourists chosen at random visited at least one of the two. (c) Verify your answer with the addition rule. (d) Find the probability that the person chosen visited exactly one.
items.answer: (a) regions: A only 10, both 2, B only 14, neither 2 (b) P(A ∪ B) = 13/14 (c) 3/7 + 4/7 − 1/14 = 13/14 ✓ (d) P(exactly one) = 6/7
items.markingKey: (a) regions: A only 10, both 2, B only 14, neither 2 (b) P(A ∪ B) = 13/14 (c) 3/7 + 4/7 − 1/14 = 13/14 ✓ (d) P(exactly one) = 6/7. Venn regions (M1 A1); probabilities (A1 A1); addition rule verified (R1 C1).

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "independent events".
items.answer: Events where the occurrence of one does not change the probability of the other: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B)

items.stem: Amara says 4 people can sit in a row of 4 chairs in 4 × 4 = 16 ways. Explain the error.
items.answer: Once a person is seated they cannot be chosen again: 4 × 3 × … × 1 = 4! = 24.
items.markingKey: Choices decrease (R1); value (A1).

items.stem: A student claims: "Independent means the events cannot happen together." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: That is mutually exclusive; independent means one does not affect the probability of the other.

items.stem: Explain why P(A ∩ B) is subtracted in the addition rule.
items.answer: Outcomes in both A and B are counted once in P(A) and again in P(B), so they must be removed once.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Outcomes in both A and B are counted once in P(A) and again in P(B), so they must be removed once. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why, for a very large population, sampling without replacement gives almost the same probabilities as with replacement.
items.answer: Removing one item barely changes the totals, so the second-pick probabilities are almost unchanged.
items.markingKey: Effect of size (R1); conclusion (R1).
